note: Archaeological chemistry (Mathakuar temple at Kusinagara, Dhamekh stupa); no location.

author: D. Mandal under G. R. Sharma, Dept of Ancient History, Culture and Archaeology, University of Allahabad
asr_identification: Kosam (Allahabad district) = Kausambi; palace on the Jamuna
evidence: 1966-67: return wall of the tower on the Jamuna traced 16 m (brick with some stone) with a parallel subsidiary wall; degenerate NBP and red ware in the debris; date undetermined
quote: The excavation at Kausambi was resumed (1963-64, p. 40) in the southern part of the Palace Area by Shri D. Mandal … The main objective of this season's work was to determine the relationship of the tower on the Jamuna with the palace
note: Kausambi = Kosam taken for granted, as Mizutani (05.05: confirmed by Sharma's excavations), asr (Cunningham) and ar. No bearing on Xuanzang's palace vihara of Udayana's image.
Sonkh excavation, 30 km SW of Mathura; not the city of Mathura.

author: S. R. Das, Department of Archaeology, University of Calcutta
evidence: 1966-67: complete plan of the panchayatana temple-complex sought; enclosure walls of two phases with niches, square corner shrines, four structural phases (Phase II platform at 2.43 m)
quote: In continuation of the previous season's work (1964-65, pp. 48-51) the Department of Archaeology of the University of Calcutta under Prof S. R. Das resumed excavation at Rajbadidanga
note: Beginning of the 1966-67 report; the identification with Raktamrittika and Karnasuvarna comes at its end (see 211).

author: S. R. Das, Department of Archaeology, University of Calcutta
asr_identification: Rajbadidanga (Murshidabad) = Raktamrittika monastery; Karnasuvarna in its neighbourhood
evidence: 1966-67: building pattern of a Buddhist monastery; seal-producing level c. 5th-6th to 8th-9th c., occupation from 2nd-3rd c.; more inscribed terracotta seals and sealings (personal names, Buddhist formulae) like those of 1964-65
quote: On the strength of the seals and other remains, the site has been identified with the illustrious Raktamrittikasangharama described by the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang in the seventh century A.D. … Accordingly, Karnasuvarna, the exact identification of which has been hitherto uncertain, is to be located in the neighbourhood of Rajbadidanga
note: Confirms Mizutani (10.08 Rangamati; 10.08.02 at Rangamati, whose name derives from Raktamrttika): Rajbadidanga is the excavated mound at Rangamati. The seal naming the monastery was found in 1964-65; this season's seals bear names and formulae only. Overturns Beglar's Dulmi/Sapharan (asr); settles the doubt in ar (Dikshit, Eastern Circle 1920-21: Rangamati doubtful as capital).
Epigraphy (Maitraka charters of Siladitya IV and V at Vadnagar); no location of Anandapura argued.

author: Chief Epigraphist, ASI
asr_identification: Nagarjunakonda (Guntur): Ikshvaku king styled lord of Sriparvata
evidence: Prakrit Brahmi inscription, 3rd c. AD, on a broken pillar reused in a well, Site 57, Sector N III: 24th regnal year of Vira-Purisadata, called Siripavatadhipati; records installation of an image
quote: belongs to the twenty-fourth regnal year of the Ikshvaku ruler Vira-Purisadata who is described therein as Siripavatadhipati and Mathariputa
note: Inscriptional link of Sriparvata with Nagarjunakonda; the report does not mention Xuanzang. Bears on Mizutani's uncertain 10.12.05 (Bhramaragiri = Faxian's Paravata/Sriparvata, proposed to be Nagarjunakonda; epig: Vogel EI 20 the same, Mirashi EI 23 near Arang/Sirpur instead); asr: Cunningham did not locate it.
Epigraphy: Kausambi and Mathura sealings with personal legends; no location.

author: S. R. Das, Department of Archaeology, University of Calcutta (seals read by B. N. Mukherjee)
evidence: 1968-69: seven trenches in the W part; three Periods, six structural phases; inscribed seals confined to Period II (Phases 3-4); 25 seals/sealings read: personal names (Jivendravarman, Sri Manjugupta …), Sri Vanika Varendrasya, one in 7th-8th-c. script, one Roman-letter seal OABORRA (cf. the Horae seal of 1962)
quote: Several complete and fragmentary inscribed terracotta seals and sealings (pl. LI B) of various shapes and sizes were obtained from the excavation, of which twenty-five could be wholly or partly read, the others being illegible. The readings were done by Dr. B. N. Mukherjee
note: None of the seals read this season names the monastery; the identification (see 240) rests on the earlier seal and the monastic plan. Agrees with Mizutani 10.08 and 10.08.02 (Rangamati).

author: S. R. Das, Department of Archaeology, University of Calcutta
asr_identification: Rajbadidanga (Murshidabad) = locale of the Raktamrittika vihara, near Karnasuvarna, capital of Gauda
evidence: 1968-69: seals palaeographically 5th-6th to 9th-10th c., mostly Phases 3-4; occupation 2nd-3rd to 12th-13th c.; building pattern of a Buddhist monastery
quote: On the basis of the seal-inscriptions, the site under excavation has firmly been identified with the locale of the famous Buddhist monastery Raktamrittika-vihara of Hiuen Tsang's accounts, which stood in the neighbourhood of Karnasuvarna, the metropolis of the Gauda kingdom of the seventh century A.D.
note: Firmly identified: the strongest IAR statement for Mizutani's 10.08/10.08.02 (Rangamati); asr (Beglar: Dulmi) overturned; ar doubted Rangamati as capital. Xuanzang's date falls within the seal-period.

author: Chief Epigraphist, ASI
evidence: Songira Chahamana inscription from Bhinmal, Vikrama 1328, reign of Chachigadeva: grant for the worship of Arbudesvara while the king ruled from Srimala
quote: SONGIRA CHAHAMANA INSCRIPTION, BHINMAL, DISTRICT JALOR.—Dated in Vikrama 1328, this Sanskrit inscription, belonging to the reign of Maharajakula Chachigadeva, registers some royal grant made for conducting worship to the deity Arbudesvara when the king was ruling from Srimala
note: 13th-c. inscription at Bhinmal naming Srimala: supports Bhinmal = Srimala/Bhillamala, Mizutani's majority view for the Gurjara capital (11.11); against Cunningham's Balmer (asr). Not linked to Xuanzang here.

author: B. K. Thapar, M. C. Joshi, N. C. Ghosh, B. M. Pande and Jassu Ram, ASI Headquarters, with the Dept of Archaeology, Bihar
asr_identification: Kankarbagh, Patna = part of the Mauryan palisade of Pataliputra
evidence: 1970-71 salvage dig in a sewer trench at Kankarbagh: fourteen wooden posts in four rows, plank-boxed and earth-rammed core of a fortification; NBP ware; like Spooner's Bulandibagh palisade (1924)
quote: On the basis of the occurrence of the N.B.P. Ware in the associated strata and the existence of similar structural remains at Bulandibagh, excavated by Spooner in 1924, it is fair to assume that the recently-exposed structure formed apart of the defences/pallisade of the Mauryan city of Pataliputra
note: Extends the palisade line of Bulandibagh (ar: Page/Spooner) S-E to Kankarbagh; agrees with Mizutani 08.02.01 (ruins about Patna), though Mizutani puts them NW towards Dinapore while Kankarbagh lies S-E of Patna. Repeated in 272.
Purana Qila excavation (Delhi).

author: Dept of Ancient History and Archaeology, University of Mysore, with the State Dept of Archaeology
asr_identification: Banavasi (North Kanara) = a city visited by Xuanzang, with the chaitya he mentions
evidence: 1970-71: brick fortification with moat and the Varada river; apsidal brick chaitya with floor-tiles in the Donigudda mound; Russet-coated Painted and imitation Rouletted wares; Kadamba pillar inscription (Kakusthavarman, Santivarman, Mrigesavarman)
quote: The ancient site, probably visited by Hiuen Tsang in the seventh century A.D., rises some four metres from the surrounding plains, and is enclosed by a fortification-wall … The structure (pls. XLV and XLVI) appears to be an apsidal temple or a chaitya (fig. 3). Traditionally, the mound contained a chaitya, the existence of which was mentioned by Hiuen Tsang
note: Implies Banavasi for Xuanzang's Konkanapura (Vivien de Saint-Martin's tentative view), against Mizutani's Annagundi (11.02, disputed; also Cunningham) and Yazdani's Kubattur. Asserted from tradition, without argument or inscription naming the place.
Tamil Nadu explorations and excavations.

Piprahwa clearance (K. M. Srivastava and A. D. P. Singh, 1970-71): stupa rebuilt, votive stupas, 17-room monastery, brick hall; no inscription and no identification with Kapilavastu yet (the Kapilavastu sealings come in later seasons).
Explorations (Mathura district) and Sonkh excavation.

author: T. S. Iyengar under Y. D. Sharma, Northern Circle, ASI
evidence: 1970-71: early medieval brick temple; central platform 25.55 x 15.3 m, raised to over 6.1 m, later enclosed by two walls in a panchayatana complex (three phases)
quote: resumed (1965-66, p. 53) the excavation of the Bhim-gada mound at Kashipur, identified as Kiu-pi-Shwanga-na of Hiuen Tsang's narrative, and rendered into Sanskrit as Govisana by Julien
note: Accepts Cunningham's identification (asr: old fort of Ujain, 1 mile E of Kashipur) as Mizutani (04.12); no inscription. The temple is later than Xuanzang.

author: T. S. Iyengar under Y. D. Sharma, Northern Circle, ASI
evidence: filling of the temple platform with pottery from PGW to early medieval; terracotta bulla like Puri-Kushan coin figures; copper coins from Mathura kings (2nd-3rd c. BC) to medieval bull-and-horseman type; plaques dated c. AD 800-1100 at Ahichchhatra
quote: It has already been mentioned (1965-66, p. 53) that the filling contained pottery ranging from the Painted Grey Ware to the early medieval period
note: Continuation of 270: long occupation of the Govisana site (04.12), as Mizutani and Cunningham.

author: K. D. Bajpai, University of Saugar (coins); Public Health Engineering Dept, Bihar (Kankarbagh)
name_in_asr: ancient Pataliputra; city of Ayodhya (Ajudhe); Kausambi
asr_identification: Kankarbagh (Patna) = Mauryan palisade of Pataliputra; coin of the city of Ayodhya found at Ayodhya; Kausambi rulers' seals and coins
evidence: Kankarbagh: wooden pillars in alignment, ornamental stone pillar, Mauryan terracottas, NBP ware; copper coin of the city of Ayodhya with legend Ajudhe (1st c. BC); Kausambi sealings of Parvata and Sivamagha
quote: COPPER COIN OF THE CITY OF AYODHYA, AYODHYA.—It bears the legend Ajudhe in Brahmi characters of the first century B.C. … It is likely that the wooden pillars formed part of the Mauryan palisade of ancient Pataliputra (see above, p. 6)
note: Kankarbagh repeats 264 (08.02.01). The Ajudhe coin shows a city called Ayodhya at modern Ayodhya (Faizabad) in the 1st c. BC; Mizutani instead prefers Führer's Fatehpur region (Aphui) for Xuanzang's A-yu-to (05.02), so a point against Mizutani, though the report does not discuss Xuanzang. Kausambi as 05.05.
